claim: The abnormal accumulation of amyloid-β and tau targets specific spatial networks in Alzheimer's disease.
source: The abnormal accumulation of amyloid-β and tau targets specific spatial networks in Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This is a primary assertion stated in the abstract that frames the study's focus.

claim: Joint independent component analysis was applied to 18F-Flutemetamol (amyloid-β) and 18F-Flortaucipir (tau) PET images to identify amyloid-β and tau networks across different stages of Alzheimer's disease.
source: In this study, we applied a joint independent component analysis to 18F- Flutemetamol (amyloid-β) and 18F-Flortaucipir (tau) PET images to identify amyloid-β and tau networks across different stages of Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Nine patterns were linked across tau and amyloid-β data.
source: Our analyses revealed nine patterns that were linked across tau and amyloid-β data.
evidence: The abstract states the number of patterns identified in the analysis.

claim: The amyloid-β and tau patterns showed a fair to moderate overlap with distinct functional networks.
source: The amyloid-β and tau patterns showed a fair to moderate overlap with distinct functional networks but only tau was associated with white matter integrity loss and multiple cognitive functions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the degree of overlap between PET patterns and functional networks.

claim: Only tau was associated with white matter integrity loss.
source: The amyloid-β and tau patterns showed a fair to moderate overlap with distinct functional networks but only tau was associated with white matter integrity loss and multiple cognitive functions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that tau, but not amyloid-β, was associated with white matter integrity loss.

claim: Only tau was associated with multiple cognitive functions.
source: The amyloid-β and tau patterns showed a fair to moderate overlap with distinct functional networks but only tau was associated with white matter integrity loss and multiple cognitive functions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that tau, but not amyloid-β, was associated with multiple cognitive functions.

claim: Amyloid-β and tau have different spatial affinities.
source: These findings show that amyloid-β and tau have different spatial affinities, which can be used to understand how they accumulate in the brain and potentially damage the brain's connections.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this finding based on the study results.

claim: The accumulation of amyloid-β and tau deposits has been implicated in the genesis of Alzheimer's disease.
source: The accumulation of amyloid-β and tau deposits has been implicated in the genesis of Alzheimer's disease (Jack et al., 2010; Jack et al., 2013; Jack et al., 2018; Jack and Holtzman, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Amyloid-β deposits appear first in neocortical regions and spread to limbic and subcortical areas.
source: whereas amyloid-β deposits appear first in neocortical regions and spread to limbic and subcortical areas (Thal et al., 2002);
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Thal et al., 2002.

claim: Tau deposits appear in the transentorhinal cortex and spread to paralimbic and neocortical areas.
source: tau deposits appear in the transentorhinal cortex and spread to paralimbic and neocortical areas (Braak and Braak, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Braak and Braak, 1991.

claim: Amyloid-β deposition occurs in highly connected brain areas, including the posterior cingulate, precuneus, anterior cingulate and medial orbitofrontal gyri.
source: Studies using positron emission tomography (PET) have shown that amyloid-β deposition occurs in highly connected brain areas, including the posterior cingulate, precuneus, anterior cingulate and medial orbitofrontal gyri (Buckner et al., 2005; Buckner et al., 2009; Jagust and Mormino, 2011; Mormino et al., 2011) already in asymptomatic stages (Palmqvist et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior PET studies.

claim: Amyloid-β deposition occurs in highly connected brain areas already in asymptomatic stages.
source: Studies using positron emission tomography (PET) have shown that amyloid-β deposition occurs in highly connected brain areas, including the posterior cingulate, precuneus, anterior cingulate and medial orbitofrontal gyri (Buckner et al., 2005; Buckner et al., 2009; Jagust and Mormino, 2011; Mormino et al., 2011) already in asymptomatic stages (Palmqvist et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Palmqvist et al., 2017.

claim: Tau deposition occurs mainly in medial and inferior temporal areas, with partial involvement of the parietal and occipital lobes in patients with mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease dementia.
source: In contrast, tau PET studies found that tau deposition occurs mainly in medial and inferior temporal areas, with partial involvement of the parietal and occipital lobes in patients with mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease dementia (Villemagne et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2016a; Johnson et al., 2016; Schöll et al., 2016; Mattsson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior tau PET studies.

claim: Amyloid-β and tau may target areas that belong to different functional networks.
source: These results suggest that amyloid-β and tau may target areas that belong to different functional networks (Hansson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is presented as a suggestion based on prior results and supported by a citation.

claim: One hundred seventeen individuals were included with 18F-Flutemetamol PET, 18F-Flortaucipir PET, structural T1-weighted MRI and neuropsychological data.
source: One hundred seventeen individuals were included with 18F-Flutemetamol PET, 18F-Flortaucipir PET, structural T1-weighted MRI and neuropsychological data.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the sample size and imaging modalities.

claim: The sample consisted of 26 cognitively normal subjects who were amyloid-β negative, in addition to 34 cognitively normal subjects, 21 patients with mild cognitive impairment and 36 patients with Alzheimer's disease dementia that were all amyloid-β positive.
source: This sample consisted of 26 cognitively normal subjects who were amyloid-β negative, in addition to 34 cognitively normal subjects, 21 patients with mild cognitive impairment and 36 patients with Alzheimer's disease dementia that were all amyloid-β positive (Figure 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the sample composition, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: A subsample of the cohort underwent resting-state functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging.
source: A subsample of this cohort also underwent resting-state functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging (Figure 1).
evidence: The Results section states that a subsample had additional imaging modalities, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Amyloid-β positivity was established using a composite cortical region normalized by the whole cerebellum, brain stem and eroded subcortical white matter on 18F-Flutemetamol PET images with a cut-off of >0.693.
source: Amyloid-β positivity was established using a composite cortical region normalized by the whole cerebellum, brain stem and eroded subcortical white matter (Landau et al., 2015) on 18F-Flutemetamol PET images with a cut-off of >0.693.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the method for determining amyloid-β positivity, with a citation.

claim: There were no significant differences in cognition between amyloid-β negative and amyloid-β positive controls.
source: As expected, there were no significant differences in cognition between amyloid-β negative and amyloid-β positive controls, but patients with mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease dementia showed worse scores in several cognitive tests.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding based on the data in Table 1.

claim: Patients with mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease dementia showed worse scores in several cognitive tests.
source: As expected, there were no significant differences in cognition between amyloid-β negative and amyloid-β positive controls, but patients with mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease dementia showed worse scores in several cognitive tests.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding based on the data in Table 1.

claim: The optimal number of components identified in the joint independent component analysis of 18F-Flutemetamol and 18F-Flortaucipir data was eleven using the minimum description length criterion.
source: The optimal number of components identified in the joint independent component analysis of 18F-Flutemetamol and 18F-Flortaucipir data was eleven using the minimum description length criterion (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the number of components identified and the criterion used, with a citation.

claim: The total variance explained by the amyloid-β components was 94.4%.
source: The total variance explained by the amyloid-β components was 94.4% and the total variance explained by the tau components was 87.4%.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the variance explained by the amyloid-β components.

claim: The total variance explained by the tau components was 87.4%.
source: The total variance explained by the amyloid-β components was 94.4% and the total variance explained by the tau components was 87.4%.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the variance explained by the tau components.

claim: Two of the independent components (IC 1, IC 9) were excluded from the analyses since they mainly included white matter areas for 18F-Flutemetamol data or off-target binding regions such as the basal ganglia for 18F-Flortaucipir data.
source: Two of the independent components (IC 1, IC 9) were excluded from the analyses since they mainly included white matter areas for 18F-Flutemetamol data or off-target binding regions such as the basal ganglia for 18F-Flortaucipir data.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states which components were excluded and why.

claim: Three of the components showed similar spatial patterns for both amyloid-β and tau, and consisted of the left inferior occipital cortex (IC 2), the superior frontal gyrus (IC 5), and medial brain regions such as the precuneus and posterior cingulate (IC 6).
source: Three of the components showed similar spatial patterns for both amyloid-β and tau, and consisted of the left inferior occipital cortex (IC 2), the superior frontal gyrus (IC 5), and medial brain regions such as the precuneus and posterior cingulate (IC 6) (Figure 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes these components with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Patients with mild cognitive impairment showed significantly higher 18F-Flutemetamol SUVRs in almost all networks compared to amyloid-β positive controls.
source: Moreover, patients with mild cognitive impairment showed significantly higher 18F-Flutemetamol SUVRs in almost all networks compared to amyloid-β positive controls.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding based on the data in Table 2.

claim: Patients with Alzheimer's disease dementia showed significantly higher 18F-Flutemetamol SUVRs in all networks compared to amyloid-β positive controls.
source: Patients with Alzheimer's disease dementia showed significantly higher 18F-Flutemetamol SUVRs in all networks compared to amyloid-β positive controls, and in the right parietal (IC 7) and lateral temporal (IC 11) networks compared to patients with mild cognitive impairment (Table 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding based on the data in Table 2.

claim: Patients with Alzheimer's disease dementia showed significantly higher 18F-Flutemetamol SUVRs in the right parietal (IC 7) and lateral temporal (IC 11) networks compared to patients with mild cognitive impairment.
source: Patients with Alzheimer's disease dementia showed significantly higher 18F-Flutemetamol SUVRs in all networks compared to amyloid-β positive controls, and in the right parietal (IC 7) and lateral temporal (IC 11) networks compared to patients with mild cognitive impairment (Table 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding based on the data in Table 2.

claim: Higher 18F-Flortaucipir SUVRs were found in the temporal (IC 3) and hippocampal (IC 8) tau networks in amyloid-β positive compared to amyloid-β negative controls.
source: Interestingly, consistent with the earliest stages of tau deposition, we found higher 18F-Flortaucipir SUVRs in the temporal (IC 3) and hippocampal (IC 8) tau networks in amyloid-β positive compared to amyloid-β negative controls.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Patients with mild cognitive impairment had significantly higher 18F-Flortaucipir SUVRs in almost all networks compared to controls that were amyloid-β negative or amyloid-β positive.
source: Patients with mild cognitive impairment had significantly higher 18F-Flortaucipir SUVRs in almost all networks compared to controls that were amyloid-β negative or amyloid-β positive (Table 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding based on the data in Table 2.

claim: Patients with Alzheimer's disease had significantly higher 18F-Flortaucipir SUVRs in all networks compared to both amyloid-β negative and positive controls.
source: Patients with Alzheimer's disease had significantly higher 18F-Flortaucipir SUVRs in all networks compared to both amyloid-β negative and positive controls, and in almost all networks compared to patients with mild cognitive impairment (Table 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding based on the data in Table 2.

claim: Patients with Alzheimer's disease had significantly higher 18F-Flortaucipir SUVRs in almost all networks compared to patients with mild cognitive impairment.
source: Patients with Alzheimer's disease had significantly higher 18F-Flortaucipir SUVRs in all networks compared to both amyloid-β negative and positive controls, and in almost all networks compared to patients with mild cognitive impairment (Table 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding based on the data in Table 2.

claim: The SUVRs of the amyloid-β networks were positively correlated with the SUVRs of all tau networks (p<0.001).
source: The SUVRs of the amyloid-β networks were positively correlated with the SUVRs of all tau networks (p<0.001).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this correlation finding.

claim: The amyloid-β medial fronto-parietal, medial, and posterior parietal networks overlapped moderately well with the posterior default-mode functional network (dice coefficients: 0.41, 0.24, 0.34).
source: For instance, the amyloid-β medial fronto-parietal, medial, and posterior parietal networks overlapped moderately well with the posterior default-mode functional network (dice coefficients: 0.41, 0.24, 0.34), whereas the amyloid-β anterior cingulate network showed a fair overlap with the anterior cingulate functional network (dice coefficient: 0.30).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states these overlap findings with specific dice coefficients.

claim: The amyloid-β anterior cingulate network showed a fair overlap with the anterior cingulate functional network (dice coefficient: 0.30).
source: For instance, the amyloid-β medial fronto-parietal, medial, and posterior parietal networks overlapped moderately well with the posterior default-mode functional network (dice coefficients: 0.41, 0.24, 0.34), whereas the amyloid-β anterior cingulate network showed a fair overlap with the anterior cingulate functional network (dice coefficient: 0.30).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this overlap finding with a specific dice coefficient.

claim: The tau networks overlapped moderately well with the extra-striate visual network (dice coefficients: 0.33, 0.30).
source: These networks were the extra-striate visual network (dice coefficients: 0.33, 0.30), the primary visual network (dice coefficient: 0.41), the limbic network (dice coefficient: 0.39) the somatosensory network (dice coefficient: 0.48); the language network (dice coefficient: 0.37) and the right fronto-parietal network (dice coefficient: 0.24).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states these overlap findings with specific dice coefficients.

claim: The tau networks overlapped moderately well with the primary visual network (dice coefficient: 0.41).
source: These networks were the extra-striate visual network (dice coefficients: 0.33, 0.30), the primary visual network (dice coefficient: 0.41), the limbic network (dice coefficient: 0.39) the somatosensory network (dice coefficient: 0.48); the language network (dice coefficient: 0.37) and the right fronto-parietal network (dice coefficient: 0.24).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this overlap finding with a specific dice coefficient.

claim: The tau networks overlapped moderately well with the limbic network (dice coefficient: 0.39).
source: These networks were the extra-striate visual network (dice coefficients: 0.33, 0.30), the primary visual network (dice coefficient: 0.41), the limbic network (dice coefficient: 0.39) the somatosensory network (dice coefficient: 0.48); the language network (dice coefficient: 0.37) and the right fronto-parietal network (dice coefficient: 0.24).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this overlap finding with a specific dice coefficient.

claim: The tau networks overlapped moderately well with the somatosensory network (dice coefficient: 0.48).
source: These networks were the extra-striate visual network (dice coefficients: 0.33, 0.30), the primary visual network (dice coefficient: 0.41), the limbic network (dice coefficient: 0.39) the somatosensory network (dice coefficient: 0.48); the language network (dice coefficient: 0.37) and the right fronto-parietal network (dice coefficient: 0.24).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this overlap finding with a specific dice coefficient.

claim: The tau networks overlapped moderately well with the language network (dice coefficient: 0.37).
source: These networks were the extra-striate visual network (dice coefficients: 0.33, 0.30), the primary visual network (dice coefficient: 0.41), the limbic network (dice coefficient: 0.39) the somatosensory network (dice coefficient: 0.48); the language network (dice coefficient: 0.37) and the right fronto-parietal network (dice coefficient: 0.24).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this overlap finding with a specific dice coefficient.

claim: The tau networks overlapped fairly with the right fronto-parietal network (dice coefficient: 0.24).
source: These networks were the extra-striate visual network (dice coefficients: 0.33, 0.30), the primary visual network (dice coefficient: 0.41), the limbic network (dice coefficient: 0.39) the somatosensory network (dice coefficient: 0.48); the language network (dice coefficient: 0.37) and the right fronto-parietal network (dice coefficient: 0.24).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this overlap finding with a specific dice coefficient.

claim: The patterns of amyloid-β and tau accumulation show a moderate spatial affinity with distinct functional networks, with the amyloid-β patterns overlapping mainly with the default-mode network, whereas the tau patterns overlap fairly well with several different resting-state networks.
source: These findings indicate that the patterns of amyloid-β and tau accumulation show a moderate spatial affinity with distinct functional networks, with the amyloid-β patterns overlapping mainly with the default-mode network, whereas the tau patterns overlap fairly well with several different resting-state networks.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this conclusion based on the overlap analyses.

claim: There were no significant correlations between the amyloid-β or tau SUVRs with the activation signals of the functional networks after adjusting for multiple comparisons.
source: There were no significant correlations between the amyloid-β or tau SUVRs with the activation signals of the previous functional networks after adjusting for multiple comparisons.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The amyloid-β networks were not significantly associated with any white matter measures.
source: In contrast to the amyloid-β networks, which were not significantly associated with any white matter measures, the tau SUVRs correlated with fractional anisotropy in several white matter tracts.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The tau SUVRs correlated with fractional anisotropy in the hippocampal cingulum tract, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, the superior longitudinal fasciculus, and the uncinate fasciculus.
source: In contrast to the amyloid-β networks, which were not significantly associated with any white matter measures, the tau SUVRs correlated with fractional anisotropy in several white matter tracts. These tracts included the hippocampal cingulum tract, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, the superior longitudinal fasciculus, and the uncinate fasciculus (Table 3, Figure 4).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states these correlations with reference to Table 3 and Figure 4.

claim: Several significant correlations were found between the tau network SUVRs and mean diffusivity in the cingulate cingulum tract, the hippocampal cingulum tract, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, and the superior longitudinal temporal fasciculus.
source: Moreover, we found several significant correlations between the tau network SUVRs and mean diffusivity in the cingulate cingulum tract, the hippocampal cingulum tract, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, and the superior longitudinal temporal fasciculus (Table 3, Figure 5).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states these correlations with reference to Table 3 and Figure 5.

claim: Worse global cognition (mini-mental state examination) was associated with increasing SUVRs in all tau networks and in almost all amyloid networks.
source: Our correlation analyses showed that worse global cognition (mini-mental state examination) was associated with increasing SUVRs in all tau networks and in almost all amyloid networks (Table 4), after adjusting for multiple comparisons.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding based on the data in Table 4.

claim: The associations between cognition and PET networks were stronger for the right parietal amyloid-β network in addition to the left inferior occipital, temporal, fronto-parietal and hippocampus tau networks.
source: These associations were stronger for the right parietal amyloid-β network in addition to the left inferior occipital, temporal, fronto-parietal and hippocampus tau networks.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states which networks showed stronger associations with cognition.

claim: Worse episodic memory (delayed recall) correlated with increasing SUVRs in almost all amyloid-β and tau networks.
source: Regarding more specific cognitive functions, we found that worse episodic memory (delayed recall) correlated with increasing SUVRs in almost all amyloid-β and tau networks.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The networks that showed a stronger association with memory were the temporal and hippocampus tau networks.
source: As expected, the networks that showed a stronger association with memory were the temporal and hippocampus tau networks.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The tau networks correlated with worse attention (trail making test A) and visuospatial (clock drawing test) abilities.
source: In contrast to amyloid-β, the tau networks also correlated with worse attention (trail making test A) and visuospatial (clock drawing test) abilities.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Attention impairment was associated with greater tau SUVRs in the left and right inferior occipital, temporal, superior and middle frontal, medial and fronto-parietal networks.
source: We found that attention impairment was associated with greater tau SUVRs in the left and right inferior occipital, temporal, superior and middle frontal, medial and fronto-parietal networks.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Visuospatial impairment correlated with increasing tau SUVRs in the left occipital, insular, medial, fronto-parietal and middle frontal networks.
source: Moreover, we found that visuospatial impairment correlated with increasing tau SUVRs in the left occipital, insular, medial, fronto-parietal and middle frontal networks (Table 4).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding based on the data in Table 4.

claim: There were no significant differences between the correlations of amyloid and tau with global cognition and delayed recall.
source: These analyses showed there were no significant differences between the correlations of amyloid and tau with global cognition and delayed recall, suggesting that the effects of both pathologies were not dissociable from each other in these specific correlations.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding from Fisher's tests.

claim: The effects of both amyloid-β and tau pathologies were not dissociable from each other in correlations with global cognition and delayed recall.
source: These analyses showed there were no significant differences between the correlations of amyloid and tau with global cognition and delayed recall, suggesting that the effects of both pathologies were not dissociable from each other in these specific correlations.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this interpretation of the Fisher's test results.

claim: Amyloid-β and tau interact with each other to increase brain damage.
source: These findings are in line with previous evidence showing that amyloid-β and tau interact with each other to increase brain damage (Ittner and Götz, 2011), and ultimately cognitive dysfunction.
evidence: The Results section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: There were significant correlations between gray matter volumes in regions that are vulnerable to Alzheimer's disease and the SUVRs of all tau networks.
source: There were significant correlations between gray matter volumes in regions that are vulnerable to Alzheimer's disease (Darby et al., 2019), and the SUVRs of all tau networks (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Supplementary file 2.

claim: There was a significant correlation between gray matter volumes and the SUVRs of the amyloid-β right parietal network.
source: Moreover, there was also a significant correlation between gray matter volumes and the SUVRs of the amyloid-β right parietal network (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Supplementary file 2.

claim: Compared to amyloid-β, tau pathology is more closely associated with neuronal loss or neurodegeneration.
source: These findings agree with previous evidence showing that, compared to amyloid-β, tau pathology is more closely association with neuronal loss or neurodegeneration (Gómez-Isla et al., 1997; Giannakopoulos et al., 2003; Bejanin et al., 2017).
evidence: The Results section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: Amyloid-β and tau start accumulating several years before the appearance of clinical symptoms.
source: There is clear evidence that these proteins start accumulating several years before the appearance of clinical symptoms and spread between brain areas with disease progression (Braak and Braak, 1998; Thal et al., 2002; Hyman et al., 2012; Jack et al., 2014; Braak and Del Tredici, 2015; Jansen et al., 2015).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: Amyloid-β and tau spread between brain areas with disease progression.
source: There is clear evidence that these proteins start accumulating several years before the appearance of clinical symptoms and spread between brain areas with disease progression (Braak and Braak, 1998; Thal et al., 2002; Hyman et al., 2012; Jack et al., 2014; Braak and Del Tredici, 2015; Jansen et al., 2015).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: Neuropathological evidence has shown that amyloid-β and tau have different spatial affinities and target distinct brain regions.
source: In line with this, neuropathological evidence has shown that amyloid-β and tau have different spatial affinities and target distinct brain regions (Braak and Braak, 1991).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior neuropathological evidence for this claim.

claim: Amyloid-β and tau have distinct accumulation patterns but also overlap in a few brain regions.
source: Our results showed that amyloid-β and tau have distinct accumulation patterns but also overlap in a few brain regions.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes the study's findings.

claim: Both amyloid-β and tau showed a fair to moderate overlap with distinct functional MRI networks, but only the tau patterns were associated with white matter integrity.
source: Moreover, both of them showed a fair to moderate overlap with distinct functional MRI networks, but only the tau patterns were associated with white matter integrity.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes the study's findings.

claim: Amyloid-β and tau deposits not only have distinct spatial patterns but their accumulation might have a different impact on functional and anatomical brain connectivity.
source: These findings indicate that amyloid-β and tau deposits not only have distinct spatial patterns but their accumulation might have a different impact on functional and anatomical brain connectivity.
evidence: The Discussion section interprets the study's findings.

claim: The amyloid-β and tau networks reflected the accumulation of pathological changes occurring in postmortem studies in patients at early and advanced stages of Alzheimer's disease.
source: These findings suggest that our amyloid-β and tau networks reflected the accumulation of pathological changes occurring in postmortem studies in patients at early and advanced stages of Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: The Discussion section interprets the study's findings in relation to neuropathological evidence.

claim: The associations between the amyloid-β and tau networks with cognition indicate that they have an important value in characterizing clinical impairment.
source: Moreover, the associations we found between the amyloid-β and tau networks with cognition indicate that they also have an important value in characterizing clinical impairment.
evidence: The Discussion section interprets the study's findings.

claim: For amyloid-β, there were significant correlations between global cognition and memory decline.
source: For amyloid-β, there were significant correlations between global cognition and memory decline, whereas for tau there were additional correlations with executive and visuospatial impairment.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes the cognitive findings.

claim: For tau there were additional correlations with executive and visuospatial impairment.
source: For amyloid-β, there were significant correlations between global cognition and memory decline, whereas for tau there were additional correlations with executive and visuospatial impairment.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes the cognitive findings.

claim: No significant associations were found between cognition and global amyloid-β PET.
source: Of note, we did not find any significant associations between cognition and global amyloid-β PET, one of the most used markers of amyloid pathology in Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Amyloid-β networks offer greater sensitivity to clinical impairment compared to conventional amyloid measures.
source: This provides further support to the use of amyloid-β networks like the ones identified in this study since they offer greater sensitivity to clinical impairment compared to conventional amyloid measures.
evidence: The Discussion section interprets the finding about global amyloid-β PET.

claim: Amyloid-β and tau pathologies have been consistently described as accumulating across interconnected brain networks in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Amyloid-β and tau pathologies have been consistently described as accumulating across interconnected brain networks in Alzheimer's disease (Seeley et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: The regions of the default-mode network could be important hubs through which the disease progresses in the brain.
source: A number of studies using functional MRI have supported this by showing that the regions of the default-mode network could be important hubs through which the disease progresses in the brain (Buckner et al., 2009; Hedden et al., 2009; Sperling et al., 2009; Sheline et al., 2010; Drzezga et al., 2011; Mormino et al., 2011; Sheline and Raichle, 2013).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: The brain regions showing highest amyloid-β accumulation coincide with the regions of the default-mode network like the precuneus and posterior cingulate.
source: Our findings indicate that the amyloid-β patterns overlapped moderately well with the anterior and posterior hubs of the default-mode network, in line with previous studies showing that the brain regions showing highest amyloid-β accumulation coincide with the regions of this functional network like the precuneus and posterior cingulate (Buckner et al., 2005; Buckner et al., 2009; Palmqvist et al., 2017).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: Tau could have a higher spatial affinity with several functional networks, which could potentially explain why it correlates with impairment in more cognitive domains in contrast to amyloid-β.
source: These findings suggest that tau could have a higher spatial affinity with several functional networks, which could potentially explain why it correlates with impairment in more cognitive domains in contrast to amyloid-β.
evidence: The Discussion section interprets the findings about tau's overlap with functional networks.

claim: Tau could be a better stage marker that reflects the progression of Alzheimer's disease through different brain regions and clinical stages.
source: Thus, as previously suggested (Blennow and Hampel, 2003), tau could be a better stage marker that reflects the progression of Alzheimer's disease through different brain regions and clinical stages.
evidence: The Discussion section suggests this interpretation with a citation to prior work.

claim: The accumulation of amyloid-β and tau converged in three brain areas such as the left inferior occipital cortex, superior frontal gyri and the precuneus.
source: Interestingly, in this study we found that the accumulation of amyloid-β and tau converged in three brain areas such as the left inferior occipital cortex, superior frontal gyri and the precuneus.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Amyloid-β exacerbates the toxic effects of tau.
source: There are different studies showing that amyloid-β exacerbates the toxic effects of tau and that tau can also mediate amyloid-β toxicity (Ittner and Götz, 2011).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: Tau can mediate amyloid-β toxicity.
source: There are different studies showing that amyloid-β exacerbates the toxic effects of tau and that tau can also mediate amyloid-β toxicity (Ittner and Götz, 2011).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: The precuneus, superior frontal and left inferior occipital gyri might be vulnerable to the combined toxic effects of amyloid-β and tau since they were present in both amyloid-β and tau network analyses.
source: Here, we suggest that the precuneus, superior frontal and left inferior occipital gyri might be vulnerable to the combined toxic effects of amyloid-β and tau since they were present in both amyloid-β and tau network analyses.
evidence: The Discussion section interprets the finding about convergence of amyloid-β and tau.

claim: Amyloid-β and tau converge in a few brain regions such as the precuneus.
source: In a previous study, it was also found that amyloid-β and tau converge in a few brain regions such as the precuneus (Sepulcre et al., 2016), in line with our findings.
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence that supports the study's findings.

claim: The temporal tau network was linked to the medial fronto-parietal amyloid-β network, which in turn overlapped moderately well with the resting-state default-mode network.
source: Another interesting finding of our joint independent component analyses is that the temporal tau network was linked to the medial fronto-parietal amyloid-β network, which in turn overlapped moderately well with the resting-state default-mode network.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding from the joint ICA.

claim: The accumulation of tau in temporal regions and alterations of the default-mode network are both important imaging markers that can be observed since early stages of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Since the accumulation of tau in temporal regions and alterations of the default-mode network are both important imaging markers that can be observed since early stages of Alzheimer's disease (Sperling et al., 2009; Sepulcre et al., 2017a; Sepulcre et al., 2017b), it is interesting to see that they both came out as connected components in our analyses, which could potentially reflect the interaction between the two proteinopathies in early disease stages.
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: The link between temporal tau and medial fronto-parietal amyloid-β networks could potentially reflect the interaction between the two proteinopathies in early disease stages.
source: Since the accumulation of tau in temporal regions and alterations of the default-mode network are both important imaging markers that can be observed since early stages of Alzheimer's disease (Sperling et al., 2009; Sepulcre et al., 2017a; Sepulcre et al., 2017b), it is interesting to see that they both came out as connected components in our analyses, which could potentially reflect the interaction between the two proteinopathies in early disease stages.
evidence: The Discussion section interprets the finding about linked networks.

claim: Compared to amyloid-β, tau accumulation in Alzheimer's disease is more closely associated with brain atrophy and white matter degeneration.
source: Our correlation analyses with gray matter volumes and white matter integrity suggest that, compared to amyloid-β, tau accumulation in Alzheimer's disease is more closely associated with brain atrophy and white matter degeneration.
evidence: The Discussion section interprets the correlation findings.

claim: Tau pathology increases both locally and distally to brain regions with synaptic connections.
source: Several studies have shown that tau pathology increases both locally and distally to brain regions with synaptic connections (Ahmed et al., 2014; Khan et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2016), and is responsible for neuronal loss (Gómez-Isla et al., 1997; Giannakopoulos et al., 2003) and axonal degeneration (de Calignon et al., 2012).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: Tau pathology is responsible for neuronal loss.
source: Several studies have shown that tau pathology increases both locally and distally to brain regions with synaptic connections (Ahmed et al., 2014; Khan et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2016), and is responsible for neuronal loss (Gómez-Isla et al., 1997; Giannakopoulos et al., 2003) and axonal degeneration (de Calignon et al., 2012).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: Tau pathology is responsible for axonal degeneration.
source: Several studies have shown that tau pathology increases both locally and distally to brain regions with synaptic connections (Ahmed et al., 2014; Khan et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2016), and is responsible for neuronal loss (Gómez-Isla et al., 1997; Giannakopoulos et al., 2003) and axonal degeneration (de Calignon et al., 2012).
evidence: The Discussion section cites prior evidence for this claim.

claim: Different tau networks were associated with lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean diffusivity in several white matter tracts, some of which were spatially close to the tau patterns, whereas others were distant.
source: Our findings are in line with previous studies since we found that different tau networks were associated with lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean diffusivity in several white matter tracts, some of which were spatially close to the tau patterns (such as the temporal tau pattern and the cingulum hippocampal tract), whereas others were distant (such as the fronto-parietal tau pattern and the inferior occipito-frontal fasciculus).
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes the white matter findings.

claim: According to the amyloid cascade hypothesis, individuals that are cognitively normal progress to mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease due to increasing amyloid accumulation, tau accumulation and MRI changes.
source: According to the amyloid cascade hypothesis proposed by Jack et al. (2013), individuals that are cognitively normal progress to mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease due to increasing amyloid accumulation, tau accumulation and MRI changes.
evidence: The Discussion section cites the amyloid cascade hypothesis.

claim: According to the recent NIA-AA criteria, AD should be regarded as a continuum rather than three distinct clinically defined entities.
source: In addition, according to the recent NIA-AA criteria (Jack et al., 2018), AD should be regarded as a continuum rather than three distinct clinically defined entities (cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment, dementia).
evidence: The Discussion section cites the NIA-AA criteria.

claim: The correlation analyses do not provide information about causality or temporal ordering between variables.
source: However, it should be noted that these analyses do not provide information about causality or temporal ordering between variables.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly acknowledges this limitation.

claim: The correlation analyses do not allow drawing definitive conclusions regarding the spread of amyloid-β and tau across different brain networks.
source: Thus, our analyses do not allow drawing definitive conclusions regarding the spread of amyloid-β and tau across different brain networks.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly acknowledges this limitation.

claim: The functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging scans were only available for a subsample of subjects in the study.
source: First of all, although we acquired different imaging sequences from the same individuals, the functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging scans were only available for a subsample of subjects in our study.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly acknowledges this limitation.

claim: The PET networks identified in the subsample with all imaging modalities were similar to the ones in the whole cohort.
source: Our secondary analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) showed that the PET networks identified in this subsample were similar to the ones in the whole cohort but it would still have been better to have the same number of subjects for all imaging modalities.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding from secondary analyses.

claim: The study is cross-sectional.
source: Secondly, our study is cross-sectional so our findings need to be replicated in longitudinal studies to assess whether the amyloid-β and tau networks can predict connectivity changes and cognitive decline over time.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly acknowledges this limitation.

claim: The weak correlations between amyloid-β and tau SUVRs with the signals of functional MRI networks was unexpected.
source: The weak correlations we found between amyloid-β and tau SUVRs with the signals of functional MRI networks was unexpected and suggests that perhaps our network analyses are not well suited to study these type of associations.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly acknowledges this unexpected finding.

claim: The study provides key evidence that amyloid-β and tau accumulate across distinct spatial networks that are clinically meaningful and closely associated with cognitive decline.
source: Despite these limitations, in this study we provide key evidence that amyloid-β and tau accumulate across distinct spatial networks that are clinically meaningful and closely associated with cognitive decline.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes the study's main contribution.

claim: The study provides important clues on the potential overlap of amyloid-β and tau with different functional networks and their association with anatomical brain connectivity as well as gray matter atrophy.
source: In addition, we provide important clues on their potential overlap with different functional networks and their association with anatomical brain connectivity as well as gray matter atrophy.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes the study's contributions.

claim: The findings shed light on which networks are preferentially targeted by amyloid-β and tau as well as their clinical value in distinguishing different disease stages and predicting cognitive decline.
source: In line with the ongoing debate on the underlying mechanisms of Alzheimer's disease (Seeley et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2012), our findings shed some light on which networks are preferentially targeted by amyloid-β and tau as well as their clinical value in distinguishing different disease stages and predicting cognitive decline.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes the study's contributions in the context of ongoing debates.

claim: All subjects gave written informed consent to participate in this study.
source: All subjects gave written informed consent to participate in this study and underwent a neuropsychological battery of tests that assessed global cognitive status (mini-mental state examination) (Folstein et al., 1975), episodic memory (delayed word list recall from the ADAS-Cog: Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale – Cognitive Subscale) (Rosen et al., 1984), attention functions (Trail Making Test A), and visuospatial abilities (clock-drawing test) (Manos and Wu, 1994).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this ethical requirement.

claim: 18F-Flutemetamol PET images were acquired 90 to 110 min after injection of 185 MBq 18F-Flutemetamol.
source: 18F-Flutemetamol PET images were acquired 90 to 110 min after injection of 185 MBq 18F-Flutemetamol and reconstructed into 4 × 5 frames using the line-of-response row-action maximum-likelihood algorithm (Palmqvist et al., 2014).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the PET acquisition protocol.

claim: 18F-Flortaucipir PET images were acquired 80 to 100 min after injection of 370 MBq 18F-Flortaucipir.
source: 18F-Flortaucipir PET images were acquired 80 to 100 min after injection of 370 MBq 18F-Flortaucipir, reconstructed into 4 × 5 frames using an iterative Vue Point HD algorithm with six subsets, 18 iterations with 3 mm filter and no time-of-flight correction (Hahn et al., 2017).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the PET acquisition protocol.
